item.title: “Monks, when the child grows up and his faculties become mature, he enjoys the five strands of sensual pleasure fully: forms cognizable by the eye…
item.description:
“Monks, when the child grows up and his faculties become mature, he enjoys the five strands of sensual pleasure fully: forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. When he sees a form with the eye, he lusts after a pleasing form and dislikes a displeasing form. He dwells with mindfulness not established on the body, with a limited mind. He does not know as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom where those evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder. Thus, in relation to the body, whichever feeling arises — pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — he delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and clings to it. Because he delights, welcomes, and clings, delight in sensual pleasure arises. With delight in sensual pleasure, there is clinging. With clinging as condition, becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 38 – Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhayasutta

item.title: “Monks, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with…
item.description:
“Monks, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Feeling … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … disenchanted with feeling … disenchanted with perception … disenchanted with formations … disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, there is knowledge: ‘Liberated.’ He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.15

item.title: Elder Sunāga: “Skilled in the mind’s signs, Knowing the taste of seclusion, Meditating, mindful, careful, He attains the non-worldly happiness.”
item.description:
Elder Sunāga:
“Skilled in the mind’s signs,
Knowing the taste of seclusion,
Meditating, mindful, careful,
He attains the non-worldly happiness.”

From: Theragāthā 1.85

item.title: “As rain seeps into a house with a faulty roof, So lust seeps into an undeveloped mind.” “As rain does not seep into a house…
item.description:
“As rain seeps into a house with a faulty roof,
So lust seeps into an undeveloped mind.”

“As rain does not seep into a house with a good roof,
So lust does not seep into a well-developed mind.”

item.title: “Knowing this body to be like foam, Realizing its mirage-like nature, Breaking Māra’s flower-tipped arrows, One goes beyond the sight of the King of Death.”…
item.description:
“Knowing this body to be like foam,
Realizing its mirage-like nature,
Breaking Māra’s flower-tipped arrows,
One goes beyond the sight of the King of Death.”

“He who gathers flowers of sensual pleasures,
With mind attached, infatuated,
Death carries him away
As a flood sweeps away a sleeping village.”

“He who gathers flowers of sensual pleasures,
With mind attached, infatuated,
Before he has had his fill of sensual pleasures,
Is overpowered by death.”

From: Dhammapada 44-59

item.title: “Monks, while I was dwelling heedful, ardent, resolute, when a thought of renunciation arose, I understood: ‘This thought of renunciation has arisen in me, and…
item.description:
“Monks, while I was dwelling heedful, ardent, resolute, when a thought of renunciation arose, I understood: ‘This thought of renunciation has arisen in me, and it leads neither to my own harm, nor to others’ harm, nor to the harm of both, increases wisdom, is not part of vexation, leads to Nibbāna.’ Monks, if I thought and pondered upon it at night, I saw no fear from that cause. If I thought and pondered upon it by day, I saw no fear from that cause. If I thought and pondered upon it both night and day, I saw no fear from that cause. But if I thought and pondered too long, my body might become fatigued; when the body is fatigued, the mind becomes disturbed; when the mind is disturbed, it is far from concentration. Then, monks, I steadied my mind internally, calmed it, unified it, concentrated it. Why was that? So that my mind would not be disturbed.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 19 – Dvedhāvitakkasutta

item.title: “Monks, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, I thought: ‘What is the gratification, what is the peril, what…
item.description:
“Monks, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, I thought: ‘What is the gratification, what is the peril, what is the escape in the case of form? … in the case of feeling? … perception? … formations? … consciousness?’ Then, monks, I thought: ‘The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on form — that is the gratification of form. That form is impermanent, suffering, subject to change — that is the peril of form. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for form — that is the escape from form.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.26
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And how, monks, is a monk one who does not bind up the wound? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye,…
item.description:
“And how, monks, is a monk one who does not bind up the wound? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he grasps the general feature, grasps the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise—he does not restrain that cause, does not guard the eye, does not practice restraint of the eye. When he hears a sound with the ear … smells an odor with the nose … tastes a flavor with the tongue … feels a touch with the body … cognizes a phenomenon with the mind, he grasps the general feature, grasps the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the mind faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise—he does not restrain that cause, does not guard the mind, does not practice restraint of the mind. Thus, monks, is a monk who does not bind up the wound.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 33 – Mahāgopālakasutta

item.title: “Householder, suppose there is a pit of glowing embers, deeper than a man’s height, filled with glowing embers that are neither flaming nor smoking. Then…
item.description:
“Householder, suppose there is a pit of glowing embers, deeper than a man’s height, filled with glowing embers that are neither flaming nor smoking. Then a man comes who desires to live, not to die, who desires happiness and loathes suffering. Two strong men grab him by both arms and drag him toward that pit of embers. What do you think, householder? Would that man twist his body this way and that?” “Yes, venerable sir. Why is that? Because he knows: ‘If I fall into this pit of embers, I will thereby meet death or deadly suffering.’” “So too, householder, a noble disciple reflects: ‘The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a pit of embers — of much suffering, much despair, and the peril is even greater.’ Having seen this as it actually is with perfect wisdom … he cultivates such equanimity.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 54 – Potaliyasutta

item.title: “One who in this world has abandoned sensuality, Left home, gone forth, With sensual desire and existence destroyed — Him I call a brahmin.” “One…
item.description:
“One who in this world has abandoned sensuality,
Left home, gone forth,
With sensual desire and existence destroyed —
Him I call a brahmin.”

“One who in this world has abandoned craving,
Left home, gone forth,
With craving and existence destroyed —
Him I call a brahmin.”

“Having abandoned the human yoke,
Transcended the heavenly yoke,
Free from all bondage —
Him I call a brahmin.”

“Having abandoned liking and disliking,
Cool, free from attachments,
A hero who conquers all worlds,
Who subdues all —
Him I call a brahmin.”

From: Dhammapada 383-423
